title: Why does my child get ly, ful and ness endings wrong?
meta_description: ly, ful and ness are added straight on to most root words, but y changes to i and ly has patterns for le, ic and truly. Here is each rule explained simply.
hero_image_alt: A short row of plain navy wooden blocks fitted end to end with one pink block resting just apart at the end, beside a blank cream card on a pale terrazzo worktop.
content_html:
Children often get the endings ly, ful and ness wrong because the national curriculum treats them as one family with a main rule and several exceptions. The Department for Education’s spelling appendix says each is added straight on to most root words, but a root ending in y changes, and ly has extra patterns for words ending in le or ic.

Key takeaways

  • The main rule is short: a suffix that starts with a consonant letter, which includes ness, ful and ly, is added straight on to most root words with no change to the last letter.
  • A root word ending in y with a consonant letter before it changes the y to i before ly, but only if the root word has more than one syllable, as in happily and angrily.
  • ly has three further patterns of its own: le becomes ly in gently, ic takes ally in basically, and truly, duly and wholly are listed as exceptions.
  • Writing the root word first and the ending second, then checking the join between them, is a useful habit for these words, because every rule here concerns where the root meets the ending.

What is the rule for adding ness, ful and ly?

The rule for adding ness, ful and ly is that each starts with a consonant letter, so each is added straight on to most root words without changing the last letter of the root. That is the wording of the Department for Education’s national curriculum spelling appendix, which groups ment, ness, ful, less and ly in a single entry in its Year 2 section. It gives enjoyment, sadness, careful, playful, hopeless and badly as examples.

In practice the root word stays whole. Sad plus ness is sadness. Plain plus ness is plainness, and the appendix prints that one with its parts shown, plain + ness. The double n in plainness is not a doubling rule at work: it is simply where the last letter of the root meets the first letter of the ending, and both letters stay.

The appendix then gives ly an entry of its own in the Years 3 and 4 section. It says ly is added to an adjective to form an adverb, that the rules already learnt still apply, and that ly is "added straight on to most root words". Examples there include sadly, completely, usually, finally and comically. The same section opens by telling teachers to pay special attention to the rules for adding suffixes.

Why do children write carefull with two l’s?

A child who writes carefull with two l’s has usually joined the whole word full to the root, when the suffix is spelt ful with one l. The appendix’s own examples, careful and playful, show the one l spelling. The likely cause is that the child knows full as a word and spells the ending as that word. The appendix does not discuss this error, and no source retrieved for this post measures how common it is.

What the appendix does establish is that ful is a suffix added to a root, and that the root stays unchanged. A practical way to hold that in mind is to treat ful as a small piece in its own right: root word, then ful, with one l.

What happens when the root word ends in y?

When a root word ends in y with a consonant letter before it, the y changes to i before ly, but only if the root word has more than one syllable. The appendix’s ly entry states this rule and gives happily and angrily as examples.

The earlier entry, for ment, ness, ful, less and ly together, lists the same condition as an exception to its straight on rule: root words ending in y with a consonant before it, but only if the root word has more than one syllable. Its examples include merriment, happiness, plentiful, penniless and happily. The appendix lists playful among its straight on examples. The y in playful follows a vowel letter, not a consonant letter, so the condition does not apply to it.

Two details are worth holding on to. The condition is about the letter before the y, and it is about the number of syllables. A child who has learnt only "y becomes i" is likely to over apply it to words such as playful.

What happens when ly goes on a word ending in le or ic?

When ly goes on a root word ending in le, the le changes to ly, and when it goes on a root word ending in ic, the ending is ally rather than ly. Both patterns sit inside the appendix’s ly entry in the Years 3 and 4 section, alongside the y to i rule above. The entry lists four exceptions to the straight on rule, and this table keeps them separate.

If the root word ends inWhat the appendix saysExamples it gives
y, with a consonant letter before itThe y changes to i, but only if the root word has more than one syllablehappily, angrily
leThe le changes to lygently, simply, humbly, nobly
icAlly is added rather than just ly, except in the word publiclybasically, frantically, dramatically
Three words listed on their ownTruly, duly, whollytruly, duly, wholly

The ic pattern explains why a child who writes basicly has followed the straight on rule faithfully. The error is a sensible one, and the fix is to learn the pattern as a separate rule, not to treat it as carelessness.

Which of these words are exceptions to the exceptions?

The words truly, duly and wholly are listed in the appendix as exceptions to the rule for adding ly, and publicly is the named exception to the ic pattern. The appendix also lists argument as an exception to the straight on rule in its Year 2 entry.

Each of truly, duly and wholly is built from a root ending in e, namely true, due and whole, and the e does not survive in the spelling. The appendix lists them as a short group to be learnt, and the sensible approach is to treat them as individual words, not as a pattern.

How can a parent help at home?

A parent can help most by keeping the practice on the child’s own school list and by making the check step cover the join between root and ending. Nothing here needs a separate list of ending words. These suggestions follow from how the method works, not from a study of suffix errors.

  1. Ask the child to say the root word first, then the ending: "care, then ful".
  2. Use the look, cover, write, check steps on the whole word, so the child writes it from memory after covering it.
  3. When checking, point to the join, the place where the root ends and the ending begins, and compare it letter by letter.
  4. If a word goes wrong again, look at whether a specific rule from this post applies before simply repeating the word.

The how spelling sticks page sets out the approach to practice in more detail. The earlier posts on prefixes and suffixes and on why a child adds the wrong ending to a word cover the other suffix rules, including ing, ed and the doubling rules, so they are not repeated here.

Frequently asked questions

Is ly always added to an adjective?

The appendix says ly is added to an adjective to form an adverb. Its examples include sadly, completely, usually, finally and comically.

Is it publically or publicly?

Publicly. The appendix gives it as the one exception to the pattern in which ally is added to root words ending in ic.

Do these rules apply to every root word?

No. The appendix says each suffix is added straight on to most root words, and it lists exceptions: argument, the y to i condition, le to ly, ic to ally, and truly, duly and wholly.

When are children expected to know these endings?

The appendix introduces ment, ness, ful, less and ly together in its Year 2 section, and gives ly a longer entry in the Years 3 and 4 section. The Years 3 and 4 section also asks teachers to pay special attention to the rules for adding suffixes.
